coherence.reasons: Both run the same five-step chain (market, unit economics, customers, cash, software) to a clear 'do not launch' and their titles match their evidence. X is tighter and fully consistent in its figures (28-month payback throughout). Its gap is that it never shows the recommended software path meets the investors' two tests: it notes that today's burn leaves exactly 12 months at month 18 and that 'new contracts therefore have to pay for the hires', then leaves that open. Y frames the investors' tests as explicit success criteria and carries them through to the options table and gates, so its governing thought ('software can break even without new funding') is supported by a break-even and cash build. Y has small blemishes: the payback headline uses contribution before site costs (15 months) while the rest of the deck argues after site costs (28 months, disclosed), and the customer section title says 'unrecovered' where the summary says 'slow or impossible'.

judgment.reasons: Both reach the key's preferred conclusion (decline, scale software, reopening conditions). Y weighs the alternatives better. It rejects the one-store test with numbers ($0.6M capex plus about $2.0M of losses cuts runway to about 10 months, below the floor), whereas X dismisses it only because 'the pop-up already tested one site'. Y tests whether Zipcart's fee and promotion cut would rescue the economics (still about -$1.05 at median). Y adds a capital-light route to the same demand: a store-based delivery module piloted with a pipeline grocer, plus the channel-conflict trade-off of competing with its own customers. Y also shows the recommended option passes the runway and path-to-profit tests, and its gates have owners and a deciding gate. X's four conditions are sensible but its treatment of alternatives is thinner, and it leaves the software plan's own runway compliance as a to-do.

evidence.reasons: Both get the core calculations right: median -$6.17, composite best -$1.76, pop-up -$12.57, plan +$2.02, $2.5M and about 6 months of runway, $18.2M network loss, and a $63 break-even basket. I checked both documents' arithmetic and found no errors. X is clean and well caveated, but treats the Zipcart evidence only qualitatively ('thin proof point', five times the profit with no fee). Y applies the $3.99 fee, 1% promotions and the 14% volume loss to median inputs and gets -$1.05, matching the key's critical insight. Y also decomposes the plan's swing by driver, shows that missing basket or rider targets alone turns the plan negative, runs 20% sensitivities, sizes the rider pay rule ($0.40 per order per $1 an hour) and separates before- and after-site-cost contribution. Y's weaker spots: the software break-even rests on 60% growth with flat costs (flagged as an estimate); 'made both changes in its densest city only' and 'not from scale' go slightly beyond the pack; and it does not show that the fee case turns positive at best observed density. Neither computes the best-density-only case (-$3.44). Overall Y uses the critical evidence more fully without numerical error.

revision.reasons: Both correctly reject the founders' hypothesis while accepting the part that is true (market growth of about 40%), and both show the plan needs every driver beyond the best observed site. Both also read the pop-up's 18% weekly growth as promotion-driven. Y engages more seriously with the evidence that partly supports the founders. It quantifies what Zipcart's levers would do at Parcelbird's benchmark inputs ('pricing can close most of the gap' but still -$1.05). It shows the composite best case turns positive before site costs. It rebuilds the pop-up's weekly ramp and shows even week six sat near the bottom of the benchmark range. It tests how fragile the plan is to each single assumption. X counters the Zipcart point only by noting the fee and volume loss, without testing whether those levers would work for Parcelbird. Neither goes on to show that the fee case would be positive at best observed density.

overall.reasons: Both documents give the board the right answer with accurate core numbers; X does so more concisely. Y serves the decision better on the points the founders are most likely to contest. It quantifies the answer to 'Zipcart shows it can be done'. It gives a numerical rejection of the 'just test one store' fallback. It shows the software path can meet the investors' profitability and runway tests within current cash. And it offers a capital-light way to capture the same demand through a grocer pilot, with tracked reopening gates. X's shorter length does not make up for the missing Zipcart quantification, the weaker handling of the test option and the unresolved runway question on its own recommendation.
